parole.significato: To set abroach; to let out, as liquor; to broach; to tap.
parole.testo: From Middle English abroche, from Norman, from Old French abroche (“to spigot”). Equivalent to a- + broach.

parole.significato: A devoted admirer and recorder of a person's words and deeds.
parole.testo: Scottish surname, from Norman, named after Beuzeville, from Beuze + -ville ("Bosi's farm"); first element from Old Norse Bosi, from Proto-Germanic *bausuz.

parole.significato: A little box, e.g. for jewellery.
parole.testo: Probably from Norman cassette. Possibly reformed by analogy with cask, thus analyzable as cask + -et. Doublet of cassette.

parole.significato: An old kind of felt hat, made from wool, down or hair, and mostly worn by boys.
parole.testo: From the Norman town name Caudebec, from earlier Caldebeck, of Scandinavian/North Germanic origin, from Old Danish kald bekkr (“cold brook”) (modern kold bæk).

parole.significato: A game played on a lawn, in which players use mallets to drive balls through hoops (wickets).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Norman croquet (“hook”), from Old Northern French croquet. Doublet of crochet, crocket, and crotchet.
From Norman decener, from Old French decenier and Latin decēnārius, from Latin decēna (“a group of ten; a tithing”). Doublet of decenary.

parole.significato: A type of traditional fruitcake. (Often as Guernsey gâche.)
Synonym of sundial or clock, a device or mechanism used to tell the hour of the day.
parole.testo: From Middle English orloge, from Norman oriloge, from Old French orloge, from Latin hōrologium (“sundial”), from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion). Cognate with French horloge, Italian orologio, and Spanish reloj. Doublet of Horologium and horologium.

parole.significato: Title for an army officer with the rank of major.
parole.testo: * As an English surname of Norman origin, from the personal name Malgier, via Old French from the Germanic name *Madalgari. parole.significato: Synonym of leprous: having leprosy or a similar skin disorder.
parole.testo: From Middle English mesel (“leprous, leper”), from Norman mesel (“leprous, leper”), from Old French mesel (“leprous, leper”), from Late Latin misellus (“leper”), from miser (“wretched, wretch”) + -ellus (“-elle”). Doublet of measles.

parole.significato: An abalone or sea-ear, particularly Haliotis tuberculata, common in the Channel Islands.
parole.testo: From Norman ormèr/ormer, variants of French ormier, contraction of oreille-de-mer, from Late Latin *auris maris (“ear of the sea”), from Latin auris (“ear”) + mare (“sea”).

parole.significato: A dolmen, cairn or similar ancient structure on the island of Jersey.
A measure of land, having varying values in Guernsey and Jersey, but approximately 18,000 square feet.
parole.testo: From Norman vergée, from Anglo-Norman vergé, vergee, originally terre vergee (“measured land”). Doublet of virgate.

parole.significato: Seaweed gathered for use as a fertilizer or fuel.
parole.testo: From Auregnais Norman vraic (“seaweed”), from Germanic. Doublet of wrack.

parole.significato: A male person regarded as unmanly or weak; a sissy.
